dedupe_keys.name: united states wildfire fatalities and the number of road exits from small communities

description: This case study tests whether the number of outward roads from a community, its egress, explains wildfire deaths in the United States. The authors, researchers at the University of California, Santa Barbara and the National Center for Ecological Analysis and Synthesis, assembled a dataset of community-level wildfire fatality counts, joined it with a nationally consistent measure of community egress, and then mapped all communities with fewer than 50,000 residents against wildfire hazard; the work is published as an open-access journal article. Coverage is national at community level. The article is free to read under a Creative Commons Attribution-NonCommercial-NoDerivatives licence. Caveats: the analysis is correlational, fatalities are rare events, and road counts do not capture road capacity, traffic or warning time. The study found that cumulative fatalities are concentrated in communities with very few exits and fall steeply up to about six non-residential roads, beyond which more routes add little; 17.7 million people live in communities below this threshold, 2.5 million of them in high wildfire hazard areas, with unexpected hotspots in Oklahoma, Florida and Hawaii. Simulation uses: a screening threshold for evacuation and emergency planning, and a validation reference for wildfire evacuation models. Related records: the Marin County coupled evacuation study (case_study-marin-county-wildfire-evacuation-tri-coupled-model) models evacuation in detail for three communities.
